title: Bells on her ankles
hookLine: a princess ties bells to her ankles and dances for Krishna, and the town calls her mad: bhakti you can hear
carry: bhakti is love you can hear
last: THE SOUL'S WEDDING TO GOD BLESSES OURS.

cards: Small brass bells, strung on a cord and tied around the ankles. Every step rings. You can't sneak anywhere wearing them; that's rather the point.
Dancers wear them on stage. In one of the songs sung in her name, a princess ties them on and dances, in public, for Krishna. The town talks.
Her husband's family is mortified. And the song hides none of it. It repeats what people said about her, and then it shrugs.
Year three heard Mira's poison cup and her treasure. Today, her feet.

teach.h: MIRA TIED BELLS ON HER FEET
teach.b: The song opens with the line people know it by, pag ghunghroo bandh Mira nachi re. The sense, in paraphrase: Mira tied bells on her feet and danced. I've made myself my Lord's own servant.
People say Mira's gone mad. My mother-in-law says I've ruined the family. And the last line: Mira's Lord is Giridhar, and she has met the undying one with ease.
First, who's speaking about her. The people, the mother-in-law, the family: the song lets them all have their say. It doesn't argue back.
It just goes on dancing. The mother-in-law's word, ruin of the family, shows the line a royal woman crossed by dancing in the open, and the song names it.
Second, the word for mad there is bawari, and in Mira's songs madness isn't only an insult. In another song she calls herself prem diwani, mad with love.
So the charge the town throws at her becomes something she wears, like the bells.
Third, the bells make devotion something you can hear.
Bhakti, the way of loving devotion, isn't only a feeling in the chest. In Mira's songs it moves the feet, keeps a rhythm, gathers a crowd.
That's why Hindus sing these songs together as bhajans, with a drum and cymbals, in temples and living rooms, and why people sometimes get up and dance.
A song about a woman who wouldn't keep still is very hard to sing sitting still.

how: Mira's songs are sung as bhajans, with drums and cymbals, in temples, homes and concert halls, and some are danced in classical and folk styles.

o: a queen who banned dancing from her husband's court
a princess-poet who danced for Krishna in ankle bells
a temple dancer who taught Krishna's songs to queens

games.q: the song of the ankle bells — tap the pairs.
p: the bells tied on her feet
mad: what the town calls her
says Mira has ruined the family

s: in the ankle-bell song, Mira argues back at the people who call her mad
the song lets them have their say, and goes on dancing.
in Mira's songs, mad can be her own word for love
she sings of herself as mad with love; the insult becomes something she wears.
Mira's songs are meant to be read silently, not sung
they're sung as bhajans, with drum and cymbals, and sometimes danced.

games.q: you're Mira. the town says you've gone mad, and your mother-in-law says you've ruined the family. what does the song do?
o: take the bells off and go home.
argue her case, line by line.
report what they said, and keep dancing.
games.why: the song quotes them, and keeps going. its last line says she has met the undying one with ease.

practice: Let one hand tap your knee very softly, in time with the breath, the way cymbals keep time at a bhajan: in, one tap; out, one tap. After a few rounds, let the hand rest and keep the beat inside, just in the breath.
If you pray, let a name of God ride that rhythm. If you don't, let the beat be enough.

wordCard.voice: Mirabai. In one of her songs she ties bells on her ankles and dances for Krishna, and when the town calls her mad, she takes the word as her own.

orig.note: Hindi. -bai is a respectful ending for a woman's name in western India; the songs mostly call her simply Mira.

carryVoice: Your line: bhakti is love you can hear. Mira tied on bells to prove it. See you tomorrow.
